name: Hardware Security
description: Security of hardware: chips, FPGAs, PUFs, fault injection, and hardware design verification.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this list is dominated by the microarchitectural reckoning of 2018. Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space (USENIX 2018) showed that the fundamental assumption underpinning system security — that kernel memory is isolated from user processes — could be broken by abusing speculative execution and CPU cache timing. The same venue and year piled on related cracks in isolation: Translation Leak-aside Buffer (USENIX 2018) defeated cache side-channel protections via the TLB, and Malicious Management Unit (USENIX 2018) argued that stopping cache attacks in software was far harder than assumed. Alongside these CPU attacks, A Bad Dream: Subverting Trusted Platform Module While You Are Sleeping (USENIX 2018) showed even dedicated trust hardware (the TPM) could be subverted through power management.

The next phase widened the attack surface and started building defenses. On the offense side, SPOILER (USENIX 2019) connected speculative load hazards to Rowhammer and cache attacks, and the community pushed into machine learning hardware with Terminal Brain Damage (USENIX 2019), followed by DeepHammer (USENIX 2020), which depleted neural network accuracy through targeted chains of DRAM bit flips. Researchers also broadened beyond pure microarchitecture: Light Commands (USENIX 2020) injected audio into voice assistants using lasers, and USBFuzz (USENIX 2020) fuzzed USB drivers via device emulation. Defensive and verification work matured in parallel — ScatterCache (USENIX 2019) randomized cache sets to thwart side channels, VRASED (USENIX 2019) delivered a formally verified hardware/software co-design for remote attestation, and HardFails (USENIX 2019) gave early insight into why software-exploitable hardware bugs evade detection. In-process isolation primitives like IMIX (USENIX 2018), Donky (USENIX 2020), and the critical PKU Pitfalls (USENIX 2020) traced an arms race over fine-grained memory protection keys.

By 2021-2022 the field professionalized into systematic analysis and automation. VoltPillager (USENIX 2021) brought hardware fault injection to bear on Intel SGX via the voltage interface, while transient-execution research turned reflective with DOLMA (USENIX 2021), Rage Against the Machine Clear (USENIX 2021), and RETBLEED (USENIX 2022), which revived speculative code execution through return instructions. Rowhammer itself proved relentless: SMASH (USENIX 2021) hammered from JavaScript despite TRR mitigations, Half-Double (USENIX 2022) reached two rows away, and ZenHammer (USENIX 2024) carried the attack onto AMD Zen platforms — a multi-year cat-and-mouse against DRAM defenses. New channels kept emerging too, from the ring interconnect in Lord of the Ring(s) (USENIX 2021) to AMD Prefetch Attacks (USENIX 2022) and ÆPIC Leak (USENIX 2022). Crucially, the toolset shifted from one-off discoveries toward automated discovery and verification — Osiris (USENIX 2021) automatically found microarchitectural side channels, and TheHuzz (USENIX 2022) fuzzed processors against golden-reference models to surface exploitable hardware bugs. The trajectory across these venues runs from a few shocking isolation breaks, through an explosion of attack surfaces and ad-hoc defenses, to a current state defined by systematic, automated hunting for hardware vulnerabilities and an unfinished battle over DRAM and speculative execution.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work shown at NDSS framed hardware security as protecting the small, resource-constrained devices at the edge of cyber-physical systems. "Securing Real-Time Microcontroller Systems through Customized Memory View Switching" (NDSS 2018) tackled memory isolation on real-time microcontrollers, while the same year already hinted at the microarchitectural direction the field would take: "Microarchitectural Minefields: 4K-Aliasing Covert Channel and Multi-Tenant Detection in IaaS Clouds" (NDSS 2018) turned the CPU's memory-order buffer into a timing covert channel, and even "Reduced Cooling Redundancy" (NDSS 2018) argued that physical infrastructure like data-center cooling is itself an attack surface.

The 2019-2020 window was dominated by two threads. One built trusted execution into hardware: "SANCTUARY: ARMing TrustZone with User-space Enclaves" (NDSS 2019) and "TIMBER-V: Tag-Isolated Memory Bringing Fine-grained Enclaves to RISC-V" (NDSS 2019) pushed enclaves down to fine-grained, per-application isolation, while "Thunderclap" (NDSS 2019) and "PeriScope" (NDSS 2019) probed the messy boundary where peripherals, DMA, and the OS meet the hardware. The second thread was the microarchitectural side-channel wave: "ConTExT" (NDSS 2020) offered a generic defense against Spectre-style transient execution, and "ABSynthe" (NDSS 2020) and "PhantomCache" (NDSS 2020) respectively automated side-channel discovery and defended caches through randomization, signaling a maturation from ad-hoc attacks toward systematic offense and principled defense.

From 2021 through 2024 the field broadened outward to the physical and analog world. A large body of signal-injection work showed that sensors and wires are exploitable hardware: "Evading Voltage-Based Intrusion Detection on Automotive CAN" (NDSS 2021), "GhostTalk" injecting voice commands over power lines (NDSS 2022), "Paralyzing Drones via EMI Signal Injection" and "Un-Rocking Drones" attacking IMU sensors (NDSS 2023), and "EM Eye," "GhostType," and camera/keyboard electromagnetic attacks (NDSS 2024). In parallel, memory-fault research stayed central with "Copy-on-Flip: Hardening ECC Memory Against Rowhammer" (NDSS 2023), and fault injection collided directly with trusted execution in "Faults in Our Bus: Novel Bus Fault Attack to Break ARM TrustZone" (NDSS 2024). Confidential-computing hardware also kept expanding, with "CAGE" extending Arm CCA to GPUs (NDSS 2024).

The most recent work shows the area consolidating around a few hard, durable problems. Rowhammer went from one-off exploits to systematic study and defense-in-depth: "FLIPPYRAM: A Large-Scale Study of Rowhammer Prevalence" (NDSS 2026) measures how widespread the weakness is, "Memory Band-Aid" (NDSS 2026) proposes low-overhead principled mitigation, and "BitShield" (NDSS 2025) hardens DNN executables against bit-flips. Trusted execution is now attacked and rebuilt at once, with "CounterSEVeillance" leaking from AMD SEV-SNP (NDSS 2025) and "RContainer" hardening containers on Arm CCA (NDSS 2025). GPUs have become first-class targets in "PhantomMap" and "Exploiting TLBs in Virtualized GPUs" (both NDSS 2026), and hardware design verification has come into its own through processor fuzzing in "ReFuzz" and "HyperMirage" (NDSS 2026). Even emerging platforms appear, with "QNBAD" targeting quantum error-mitigation (NDSS 2026), showing that as new hardware ships, the security community is now probing it almost immediately.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats hardware itself as the attack surface, not just the software running on it. In 2018, "FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks" (S&P 2018) showed that a tenant sharing a cloud FPGA could read a co-located design's power signature entirely from the reconfigurable fabric, while "Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2018) demonstrated that early Rowhammer mitigations were already being routed around. "Grand Pwning Unit" (S&P 2018) pulled the GPU into microarchitectural attacks, and "Blue Note" (S&P 2018) showed acoustic interference could physically disrupt hard drives — together sketching a field that spanned memory disturbance, side channels, and analog effects.

The 2019 discovery of "Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution" (S&P 2019) reoriented the whole area around transient execution, and a wave of follow-ons quickly filled it in: "RIDL" (S&P 2019) leaked in-flight data, "Port Contention for Fun and Profit" (S&P 2019) mined SMT scheduling, and "Theory and Practice of Finding Eviction Sets" (S&P 2019) put cache-attack primitives on rigorous footing. In parallel the Rowhammer thread deepened, with "Exploiting Correcting Codes" (S&P 2019) showing even ECC memory was not a safe defense. By 2020 the attacks turned inward on trusted hardware: "Plundervolt" (S&P 2020) used voltage scaling as a software fault-injection weapon against SGX, "TRRespass" (S&P 2020) broke the vendors' Target Row Refresh mitigation, and "RAMBleed" (S&P 2020) escalated Rowhammer from corruption to reading secret bits.

The early 2020s show the field maturing on both offense and defense. "PLATYPUS" (S&P 2021) and "CacheOut" (S&P 2021) refined power and cache leakage, while defensive and constructive work grew up alongside it: "DifuzzRTL" (S&P 2021) brought differential fuzzing to hunt CPU bugs before silicon, "Hardware-Software Contracts for Secure Speculation" (S&P 2021) tried to formalize what a safe processor even promises, and "Systematic Analysis of Randomization-based Protected Cache Architectures" (S&P 2021) audited proposed defenses. That momentum carried into 2022 with "BLACKSMITH" (S&P 2022) bypassing the latest in-DRAM Rowhammer defenses in the frequency domain, "ProTRR" (S&P 2022) proposing a principled counter, and "DeepSteal" (S&P 2022) using memory faults to steal neural-network weights.

The most recent work at S&P 2026 shows the area circling back to physical hardware and confidential computing while keeping its formal edge. "TEE.Fail" (S&P 2026) breaks trusted execution environments with a DDR5 memory-bus interposer, and "BreakFAST" (S&P 2026) mounts a confused-deputy attack on AMD's Infinity Fabric to defeat SEV-SNP, signaling that TEEs remain the central battleground. Classic threads persist and mutate — "GDDRHammer" (S&P 2026) carries Rowhammer to modern GPUs, and "VMSCAPE" (S&P 2026) and "Rain" (S&P 2026) revive transient-execution leaks in cloud settings. At the same time, the defensive and verification side has grown teeth: "Goldilocks and the Three P-States" (S&P 2026) offers formal leakage guarantees against Hertzbleed, "Interplay of Efficient Model Checking and Secure Processor Design" (S&P 2026) verifies secure speculation, and "SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About Bootloader Security" (S&P 2026) consolidates a foundational layer — evidence of a field now attacking hardware at the bus level while trying to prove its defenses correct.

ccs.narrative:
Hardware security at CCS has been defined by the speculative-execution revolution and its aftershocks. The 2018-2019 period produced some of the most-cited CCS papers ever: ret2spec (CCS 2018), ZombieLoad (CCS 2019), Fallout (CCS 2019), and SMoTherSpectre (CCS 2019) collectively mapped the transient-execution attack landscape on Intel processors. Screaming Channels (CCS 2018) added an RF-side-channel dimension, and Rendered Insecure (CCS 2018) extended hardware attacks to GPUs. Nemesis (CCS 2018) closed the circle by targeting SGX via interrupt timing.

Fault-injection attacks against neural networks and TEEs formed a parallel track. Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks (CCS 2018) showed row-hammer style bit flips can misclassify DNN outputs, while VoltJockey: Breaching TrustZone by Software-Controlled Voltage Manipulation over Multi-core Frequencies (CCS 2019) induced faults in TrustZone via software-controlled voltage scaling. One Glitch to Rule Them All: Fault Injection Attacks Against AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization (CCS 2021) extended glitching to AMD SEV.

Defense research moved toward formal verification of hardware contracts. InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis (CCS 2020) automated the find-and-fix cycle for Spectre gadgets. Exorcising Spectres with Secure Compilers (CCS 2021) proved that compiler mitigations can be formally sound against an attacker with full microarchitectural knowledge.

milestones.title: ret2spec: Speculative Execution Using Return Stack Buffers
milestones.note: Discovered a Spectre variant exploiting return-stack-buffer misprediction to leak arbitrary memory.

milestones.title: Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical
milestones.note: Made GPU side-channel attacks practical, leaking sensitive data from graphics and ML compute workloads.

milestones.title: Screaming Channels: When Electromagnetic Side Channels Meet Radio Transceivers
milestones.note: Found that RF transceivers on SoCs broadcast side-channel leakage, enabling wireless key extraction.

milestones.title: Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks
milestones.note: Demonstrated hardware fault injection can reliably subvert DNN inference results.

milestones.title: ZombieLoad: Cross-Privilege-Boundary Data Sampling
milestones.note: Leaked cross-privilege data by exploiting CPU load-buffer fill behavior during transient execution.

milestones.title: VoltJockey: Breaching TrustZone by Software-Controlled Voltage Manipulation over Multi-core Frequencies
milestones.note: Broke ARM TrustZone isolation using software-controlled CPU voltage to induce exploitable hardware faults.

milestones.title: InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis
milestones.note: Automated Spectre gadget detection and repair using formal microarchitectural analysis.

milestones.title: One Glitch to Rule Them All: Fault Injection Attacks Against AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization
milestones.note: Broke AMD SEV's memory encryption and register protection with voltage glitch attacks on the secure processor.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list mark the moment hardware security became a mainstream systems concern rather than a niche electrical-engineering topic. In 2018, "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) showed that out-of-order execution could leak protected kernel memory to unprivileged code, breaking the memory isolation that all software trusts. It arrived alongside a wave of related microarchitectural work: the "Translation Leak-aside Buffer" TLB attacks (USENIX 2018), "ret2spec: Speculative Execution Using Return Stack Buffers" (CCS 2018), and side channels reaching beyond CPU caches into GPUs ("Rendered Insecure", CCS 2018) and even radios ("Screaming Channels", CCS 2018). In parallel, the physical and DRAM side of the field advanced with "Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2018) and the first "FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks" (S&P 2018), which showed that even remote, shared programmable hardware could leak secrets.

The 2019 wave turned these one-off discoveries into whole attack families. "Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution" (S&P 2019) generalized transient-execution leakage to almost any modern CPU, and a cluster of Meltdown-style data-sampling attacks quickly followed — "RIDL: Rogue In-Flight Data Load" (S&P 2019), "ZombieLoad" (CCS 2019), and "Fallout: Leaking Data on Meltdown-resistant CPUs" (CCS 2019) — showing the problem persisted even on supposedly patched chips. Researchers also sharpened the underlying primitives, with "Theory and Practice of Finding Eviction Sets" (S&P 2019) and new contention channels in "Port Contention for Fun and Profit" (S&P 2019) and "SMoTherSpectre" (CCS 2019). Two important shifts happened here: defenses became first-class research targets (randomized caches in "ScatterCache", USENIX 2019; the demonstration in "Exploiting Correcting Codes" that ECC does not stop Rowhammer, S&P 2019; hardware-bug tooling in "HardFails", USENIX 2019), and machine-learning models emerged as victims, with "Terminal Brain Damage" (USENIX 2019) using hardware fault attacks to degrade deep neural networks.

By 2020-2022 the field matured toward software-triggered physical attacks and cross-domain fusion. "Plundervolt" (S&P 2020) and "PLATYPUS" (S&P 2021) weaponized voltage and power interfaces from software to break Intel SGX, while "LVI" (S&P 2020) inverted Meltdown to inject attacker data into a victim. Rowhammer kept escaping its defenses through "TRRespass" (S&P 2020), "RAMBleed" (S&P 2020, which reads rather than writes bits), and "BLACKSMITH" (S&P 2022, frequency-domain hammering). The ML-hardware intersection deepened with "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) and "DeepSteal" (S&P 2022), which used memory bit flips to steal or destroy model weights, and "CrossTalk" and "CacheOut" (both S&P 2021) pushed transient leakage across cores.

The most recent work, concentrated at NDSS 2026, shows the field broadening from a few CPU-centric threats to a wide, tool-driven landscape. Rowhammer research has shifted from new exploits to measurement and principled defense, with "FLIPPYRAM: A Large-Scale Study of Rowhammer Prevalence" and "Memory Band-Aid: A Principled Rowhammer Defense-in-Depth". Verification and fuzzing of hardware itself is now central, seen in "ReFuzz: Reusing Tests for Processor Fuzzing with Contextual Bandits" and "HyperMirage: Direct State Manipulation in Hybrid Virtual CPU Fuzzing". Attacks continue to spread across accelerators and platforms — "PhantomMap: GPU-Assisted Kernel Exploitation" and "Exploiting TLBs in Virtualized GPUs for Cross-VM Side-Channel Attacks" carry GPU and TLB threats into the cloud — while newer frontiers appear in "QNBAD" (quantum-noise backdoors), "DualStrike" (keystroke eavesdropping and injection), and "SECV: Securing Connected Vehicles with Hardware Trust Anchors", signaling a move from discovering isolated bugs toward systematically testing, measuring, and defending hardware across ever more domains.
